_readme: WHAT THE IMAGE SHOWS - the plain-language visual description of each cover, one paragraph, three to five sentences. This is the top block of the prompt because the subject is the most important instruction in it: everything below is how to draw it, nothing above it says what to draw. Authored by hand, never generated. Constraint enforced by prompts_chatgpt.py --check: no digit characters, so every number in a prompt stays inside the FRAME MATH section where it can be audited.

issues.1: An endless stone spiral seen from just above its rim: a single road enters at the left, crosses the frame dead level, and then winds itself inward and downward through a stack of shrinking rings. Each ring is a wall of cut stone, thinner and darker than the last, and the last is barely wider than a coin. Nothing else is in the frame — no figure, no sky, no horizon. The whole picture is the fact that a road which runs one direction ends up going down.
issues.2: A hooded figure, seen from directly behind, climbing a stone staircase that turns away and upward to the right. The figure is tiny and the stair it climbs is enormous, its treads wide enough for six. The stair leaves the top right corner, so the frame never shows where it ends. There is no face to read and no gesture to interpret; the entire image is one small body committing to a large climb.
issues.3: Four ruined doorways, one inside the next, receding into a dark throat of broken stone. Each arch is smaller than the one in front of it and set a little further off centre, so the tunnel leans as it goes and the eye slides inward instead of standing still. The stonework is chewed and unfinished — arches missing their keystones, jambs cracked through. The deepest opening is nearly black.
issues.4: A heavy stone doorframe with exactly one opening in it, and the opening is not in the middle. Two arcs of different radius meet off axis, so the shape refuses to mirror itself anywhere: no vertical line, no horizontal line, nothing you could fold the frame along to make the two halves agree. The stone is thick, plain and worked. This is the plainest object in the series and the least symmetric, and those two facts are the same fact.
issues.5: A single ordinary chair — four legs, a flat seat, a plain back — split down the middle by a hard vertical seam and mirrored so exactly that the two halves no longer agree. Left of the seam it is drawn one way; right of the seam the same chair is drawn slightly differently, and neither half is the odd one. The background is dense ink-work that also mirrors and also refuses to resolve. Keep looking and the thing keeps declining to become a single object.
issues.6: A tower that fills the whole upper frame and runs out of the top of the image, so you cannot see how tall it is. At the bottom edge, on its own, one small cloaked figure reaches up toward it. Every scrap of detail in the frame is spent on the tower — courses, arches, ledges, a dark opening somewhere high up — and the figure is almost nothing. The size difference is the entire content; there is no other event in the picture.
issues.7: Two storks standing face to face across a hard vertical seam, beaks open, in the middle of an argument. Everything left of the seam is drawn in cold light — cyan, pale blue — and everything right of it in hot light — orange, red, magenta — and the seam itself is a hard edge with no fade across it. Their long beaks cross the seam and overlap. Nine voices are arguing and the picture only has room for two of them.
issues.8: One ornate brain-like mass, symmetrical to a fault, cut straight down the middle by a single hard vertical seam. The entire left hemisphere is cold — cyan line-work only — and the entire right hemisphere is hot — magenta and orange only — and neither side uses the other's colour anywhere. Inside each half the line-work folds in on itself: nested chambers, and smaller chambers inside those. This is the cover of the whole argument, so it has to look like a decision rather than an accident.
issues.9: One large key — bow, shaft, wards and all — assembled entirely out of hundreds of small identical keys packed in a brick lattice so tight they read as one continuous metal surface. From across the room it is unmistakably a key. Put your nose against it and it dissolves: every component is the same tiny key, the same size, the same angle. Nothing is drawn onto the key. The key is made of keys.
issues.10: A real comic page: six panels in two rows of three, on cream paper, in black brush line, with screentone dots for every shadow. A single figure walks east through all six panels in the order you read them, so the reading direction and the travel direction are the same direction. Each panel carries three rows of lettering that are letter-shaped and spell nothing. The drawing is right and the words are wrong.
issues.11: A spinal column taken apart and reassembled on a widening spiral, vertebra after vertebra, each one lit from inside so it glows at its own centre. It reads as a mechanism being built rather than as a body posed for a picture: the bones climb, turn, and climb again. Nearly a full turn of spiral and it has still not come back to where it started. All the light in the frame comes from the bones themselves; nothing outside the column is lit at all.
issues.12: Eight identical standing figures arranged in a perfect ring, each one a closed shape with a single piece cut out of it, and each cut-out a slightly different shape. Nothing else is in the frame. The repetition is the point: one form, eight times, no variation in the bodies and one variation in the wound, so the ring reads as still and ceremonial. Seen from the centre, none of them stands in front of another.
issues.13: One central form with exactly three wings, caught one twentieth of a turn past the end of its own stroke. The three wings are identical and set a third of a circle apart, tips on one circle. Because there are exactly three and they are exactly equal, the image reads as one movement caught mid beat rather than as decoration. Behind the form, ink laid down to carry the mood — loose, hot, and clearly secondary to the wings.
issues.14: A hub and spoke diagram so densely labelled that the labels have collided: leader lines cross, text blocks overlap, and the outer ring breaks down into illegible noise exactly where it should have been clearest. Everything is drawn correctly — nodes evenly spaced, rings concentric, rules straight — and the result is unreadable at thumbnail size, which is the warning the picture is making. Read it at full size and you still cannot finish it.
issues.15: One beam of pale wine-red light crosses the whole frame from the bottom left corner to the top right corner and strikes a standing glyph-form at the exact centre. The glyph is the only thing in the image the beam touches; everything outside the cone stays dark. The cone widens as it travels, so the light looks poured rather than shone. There is no source for it and nothing to catch it afterwards.
issues.16: Two robed figures standing face to face, both bent forward, both leaning toward a single point in the space between them. One has a hand against the other's chest. Neither face is visible; both hoods are down. The space between them holds the whole image and the rest of the frame is empty and still. This is the last time it happens in the series, so it is drawn with nothing else in it at all.
issues.17: A small calm figure, seen from behind, holding out a second form that is coming apart at its edges. Loose fragments drift off the failing form in a halo while its core stays perfectly intact. The figure is not struggling and not running — it is holding something already lost. Danger has to be visible as decay around the rim, or the picture ends up selling the idea instead of charging for it.
issues.18: One large eye-form with four pupils instead of one, arranged two by two, each pupil showing the same scene in a different horizontal band of colour: through one you see it in red, through the next in orange, the next in blue, the last in a fourth band. Four passes of the same vision at once. The eye is otherwise beautifully and slightly absurdly drawn. More eyes means more perception, and the picture has to feel like a cost rather than a gain.
issues.19: A ring of light, bright and hard edged, and inside it a hole of absolutely pure black shaped like a person standing. The black is not dark grey and not shadow — it has no texture at all, nothing for the eye to catch on — and the ring around it is the only thing in the frame with any structure. The void is where a second person should be. It is the loudest shape available and it is drawn with the least material.
issues.20: One ordinary rose, rendered with near photographic care in greyscale, sitting dead centre of the frame on a grid that recedes to a low horizon. Every petal is separated, every fold is shaded, and the shading is real tonal gradation with a soft cast shadow. There is nothing else — no figure, no ornament, no frame device, no border. This is the only image in the series where the object is entirely true, and the emptiness around it is deliberate.
issues.21: Six figures of different heights caught in the same instant — mid stride, mid turn, mid reach, mid fall — none of them posing, all of them facing east. They share a frame but not a pose, and every one of them sits on a different diagonal so nothing lines up into a rank. It reads as one moment photographed rather than as a group arranged. The horizon is low and there is a great deal of empty ground under them.
issues.22: A caduceus and a double helix standing side by side on a shared plinth, drawn to exactly the same standard of finish so that neither one wins. Both are complete and both are accurate; the question the picture asks is which is the truer symbol, and the picture refuses to answer it. The background is a receding grid with nothing on it at all. Old, equal, and unresolved.
issues.23: An entire panel of interlaced crimson and gold filigree with nothing depicted inside it at all. The strands cross, knot and open again at three different densities; there is no figure, no object, no ground, no horizon, no light source. It has to be beautiful enough that the emptiness reads as a choice rather than an omission. The hardest thing to draw is nothing, and that is the whole commission.
issues.24: An engraved book plate: a gold double ruled border with corner ornaments, a heavy outer rule, and a completely blank cartouche at the centre where a name would go. The blank centre is not unfinished — it is the subject, and it is the only quiet area in the frame. Gold remembers every hand. This plate has not had one yet, and it is waiting in a way that looks deliberate.
issues.25: A laboratory instrument built from concentric dials with a single sweeping needle caught part way round. Every scale is marked with tick strokes that look exactly like numbers without being any of them. It should read as real equipment, the kind with a maker's plate on it — but it cannot name itself, and neither can the picture, so all the scales are silent. The needle is the only thing in the frame that moves.
issues.26: Eight identical circular subsystems on a single ring around one empty core, connected by thin radial spokes. Every node face is blank — no fill, no label, no number, no icon. The core is empty too, and that is the point: the machine explains itself everywhere except the one place where it would have to explain what it is. The layout is the message, and it is completely reusable as it stands.
issues.27: A nine cell system diagram with correct structure and visibly bad execution: flat mustard fills, thick clumsy outlines, no finesse, no gradient, no shadow, nothing that earns its place. The proportions are right and the connections are right and it is still ugly. Do not improve it. The point is that a diagram can be ugly and still be right, and that a beautiful one can be wrong.
issues.28: An assembly diagram in which four badge shaped callouts float near the corners, each one connected by a thin leader line — and each leader line lands on empty white space. The boxes the labels point at are empty, but the boxes themselves are there, drawn and measured, waiting for names that were never supplied. Asked to annotate, it produced glyph shaped holes.
issues.29: A single polyhedron with exactly eight wheels arranged evenly around it, drawn as pure line work on a dark ground. No key, no legend, no title block, no dimension, no arrow, no callout, no caption. Nothing else in the frame. This is the reusable version — the empty version — and it is the one that can be labelled by hand afterwards, which the labelled version can never be.
issues.30: An engraved book plate with a heavy gold border and corner ornaments, its blank centre now carrying one line of crisp capital lettering: AMPHETAMEMES. The letters are clean, centred, evenly tracked, and they are the only text in the image. Everything else in the plate is ornament and rule. The word is drawn the way a word should be drawn: correctly, once, with nothing competing with it.
issues.31: A numbered colour key in a single column — swatches in a row, a numeral beside each — standing beside the eight node ring diagram that the swatches belong to. Swatch, index mark and node sit on one shared grid, so the key and the diagram visibly agree. This is what a finished legend looks like: numbered, keyed, real, and reusable by whoever picks the file up next.
issues.32: An ornate violet and gold filigree panel, and somewhere in the lower left a region of the pattern is dense enough that it almost suggests a figure — and then it stops. It is beautiful, it is completely uninformative, and a viewer cannot tell what it is meant to be showing. No focal object, no figure, no ground plane, no horizon. It chose to be pretty instead of correct, and the picture is about that choice.
issues.33: A finished comic page in three rows of panels on cream paper, in black ink, with one magenta accent used sparingly. Nine panels carry four beats in reading order: a whirl, a hand, a small figure, a tunnel. The panel grid is real, the gutters are real, and the colour script is real and consistent — and this is the only image in the series that is already a page rather than a cover. Between the last panel and nothing, the page holds a pause open.
issues.34: The ground is inverted here: a cream white paper field instead of black, with the magenta as the only ink. A small hooded figure stands at the bottom, seen from behind and entirely alone, and a single magenta eye form hangs exactly above its head on the same vertical axis. The two are one statement. Most of the frame is empty, and the emptiness is the distance between them.
issues.35: A tall vertical column of small chevrons stacked up the centre of the frame, and every single one of them points east. The column itself is perfectly vertical; the direction inside it never changes. At a glance it is a ladder, a spine or a stack of arrowheads, and you only notice the contradiction if you read it. Every mark the same size, every mark disagreeing with the axis it sits on.
issues.36: Two outlined triangles, one upright and one inverted, overlapping so that they share a single vertex. Six of the seven points sit on one circle at even intervals; the seventh is the lower vertex of the inverted triangle, and it is off that circle by a few degrees and visibly wrong. Hold the frame still and empty around it and the mistake is the loudest thing in the image.
issues.37: An empty tailored suit on a hanger, the shoulders holding their shape, and inside the hood shaped opening where a head would be there is nothing at all — no face, no shadow, no hint of one. It is drawn with fewer strokes than anything else in the series: one confident contour per edge, no hatching, no ornament, no background incident. Somebody built this suit. The picture does not say who.
issues.38: A hooded figure seen from behind, so close that the hood fills the frame and runs off the top of it. The hood is a solid black mass with no interior detail whatever — not a hint of a shoulder, not a fold of cloth. A single thin red rim light runs down the right hand contour and nowhere else. One dominant shape, no secondary objects, no background incident.
issues.39: A single large green eye low in the frame, half lidded, looking down a corridor of blue walls lit at intervals by orange lamps. Blue and orange do all the work; the green is the only third colour in the image and it appears nowhere else, so the eye holds the whole frame together. The corridor converges behind it. It is watching, and nothing in the picture is watching back.
issues.40: The entire composition printed in a single crimson ink on cream paper — no second plate, no grey, no black, no second colour anywhere. A road runs east across the frame toward one standing figure, and everything else is carried by three line weights and four dot densities and nothing more. Strip it to a single hue and it gains value. It will still work.
issues.41: An empty amber rectangle: one outer rule, one inner margin rule, four corner crop marks, and nothing at all inside the field. Pure geometry, zero text, nothing placed in the frame — a skeleton you can label yourself. It has to look deliberate rather than unfinished, which means the proportions are exact, the crop marks are correct, and the empty centre is clean.
issues.42: A complete infographic sheet: a title band across the top, a year, a subtitle, section headers down one side, a topology diagram in the middle, a legend, and a paragraph of body copy at the foot. The layout is entirely correct — grid, hierarchy, alignment, spacing all right — and every word in it is wrong, word shaped and nothing more. The sheet survives on layout alone, and that is what the picture is examining.
issues.43: A node link graph of thirty circles in three distinct shapes and three colours, scattered across the frame by a force simulation rather than arranged by hand. Three clusters pull on each other, edges cross, and the layout is slightly untidy in the way generated output always is. One library name is printed small in the lower right corner: Chart.js. It knows the tool it is imitating.
issues.44: An engineering blueprint sheet: nine stacked layers drawn in cross section, each one labelled, separated by even gaps, with dimension rules down one side and along the foot, a set of leader lines, tick marked scales, and a title block in the corner with six empty fields. Every rule is thin, straight and parallel to an edge. The labels are real. Nothing has been built yet; this is the drawing that comes first.
issues.45: Nine figures of the same build, caught mid gesture at nine different stages of the same motion, layered front to back along one diagonal so that every one of them reads separately. The nearest is nearly resolved; the furthest is barely more than an intention. The stagger means no figure hides behind another, and the diagonal carries the eye from the near corner to the far one. Everyone it ever split off, in one frame.
issues.46: A tall narrow stack of five slabs rising from a base, each one a little smaller than the one below it, so the column tapers as it rises. On the very top, one small shape perches — the only living thing in the frame. No ground, no horizon, no background incident; the stack and the perched shape are the entire image. The sacrifice, drawn as a place you could stand on.
issues.47: A tree trunk filling the frame, cropped at the base and at the crown, and the fissures in the bark resolve into a single calm face — eyes at the same height, a mouth below them, all of it formed by the cracks themselves and not one stroke added on top. At the crown, a thin halo of gold rays. The face must not be drawn onto the bark; it has to be what the bark already was.
issues.48: One symmetrical being at the exact centre of the frame, absolutely still, crowned in fire that reaches up past its shoulders. Its left half is cyan; its right half is magenta and gold; the seam between them is a single hard vertical line with no gradient across it. No motion anywhere in the image — every edge is vertical, horizontal, or on a ray of the crown. This is the cover that states the thesis, so it has to feel like an ending rather than a beginning.
